client: I've been avoiding this one café near my apartment for weeks now, and it's starting to mess with my daily routine because it's honestly the most convenient place to grab coffee before work. Every time I even think about walking in there, my heart starts racing and I get this tight feeling in my chest, like I can't breathe properly. It's where my ex and I used to meet all the time, and I don't know... I feel kind of stupid even saying that out loud, like I'm not sure therapy can really fix something that seems so specific and kind of irrational.
therapist: There's nothing stupid about what you're feeling — your body and mind are doing exactly what they're designed to do, which is protect you from something that was once associated with real emotional pain. Those physical sensations like the racing heart and tightness in your chest are very real, and it makes complete sense that your nervous system has linked that café to grief and loss. I'm also curious — when you call it "irrational," what do you think *should* be happening instead, and where did that expectation come from?

client: I guess I think I should just be over it by now — it's been like four months since we broke up, and most of my friends seem to think that's more than enough time to move on. That expectation probably comes from them, honestly, or just this general idea that you're supposed to be functional and not let something like a coffee shop derail your whole morning. But hearing you say my nervous system is just trying to protect me... I don't know, it doesn't make me feel less embarrassed about it, but it does make it feel slightly less like a personal failure.
therapist: There's no universal timeline for grief, and the fact that your friends have moved on from *watching* your breakup doesn't mean you should have moved on from *living* it — those are very different experiences. I love that you noticed the shift from "personal failure" to something slightly more neutral, because that small change in how you're framing it is actually really meaningful. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you and said they were still hurting four months after a breakup, what would you say to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that four months isn't that long and that they don't have to rush themselves, and I'd mean it genuinely. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself it just... doesn't land the same way, like there's this double standard I can't seem to turn off. I know what you're going to say — that I should treat myself the way I'd treat a friend — and I get it intellectually, but it feels almost impossible to actually believe it when it's about me.
therapist: You're already one step ahead, which tells me part of you genuinely *wants* to extend that compassion to yourself — the barrier isn't understanding, it's something deeper that makes you feel less deserving of the same kindness you'd freely give someone else. That gap between knowing something intellectually and actually *feeling* it is one of the most common and frustrating experiences people bring to therapy, and it's worth exploring rather than just pushing through. What do you think that double standard is protecting you from — what might happen if you actually let yourself off the hook?

client: Honestly, I think if I let myself off the hook, I'd have to admit that I'm still really hurt and that I miss him, and that feels scarier than just being angry at myself for being irrational. Like, self-criticism is almost easier because it gives me something to do with all this feeling — if I'm busy judging myself, I don't have to just sit with the grief. I haven't really said that out loud before and it's a little uncomfortable to hear myself say it now.
therapist: What you just said took real courage, and it's genuinely one of the most insightful things a person can recognize about themselves — that self-criticism can actually function as a kind of armor against something that feels even more vulnerable. You've essentially identified that the "irrationality" you've been judging yourself for is covering something much more tender, which is just honest, human grief and longing. I'm curious — now that you've said it out loud, what does it feel like to let that be true for a moment, without immediately judging it?

client: It feels sad, mostly — like a kind of quiet sadness that's different from the anxious, self-critical feeling I'm more used to. There's something almost relieving about it but also kind of exposing, like I've taken off something I didn't realize I was wearing. I'm not sure I can hold that feeling for very long before the judging voice comes back in, though.
therapist: That image of taking off something you didn't realize you were wearing is really beautiful and precise — and the fact that you could hold that quieter, truer feeling even for a few moments is genuinely significant, because you've just shown yourself that you *can* access it. The judging voice coming back in isn't a failure; it's just a very practiced habit that developed to keep you safe, and habits can be gently loosened over time with exactly the kind of awareness you're already showing. I'm wondering — what do you think that quieter, sadder part of you most needs right now, if the judging voice weren't allowed to answer for it?

client: I think that part of me just needs to feel less alone with it, like it wants someone to acknowledge that losing him was actually a real loss and not just something I should quietly get over. It's strange because I have people around me, but I still feel this loneliness around this specific thing, like no one really knows how much that relationship meant to me. I didn't expect to feel that when you asked — I thought I'd say something like "I need to go back to that café" or something more practical, and instead it's just... that.
therapist: What just came up for you is far more important than any café, and I want to make sure you hear this clearly: losing that relationship was a real loss, it mattered, and you are allowed to grieve it as fully as it deserves. There's something really poignant about feeling lonely in the middle of having people around you — it speaks to how much you've been carrying this quietly, maybe protecting others from the weight of it, or protecting yourself from feeling like too much. I'm curious — is there anyone in your life you think could hold this with you if you let them see how much it actually meant to you?

client: There's maybe one friend, my friend Dara, who I think could handle it without making it weird or trying to immediately fix it. But I get really scared that if I show her how much I'm still affected by this, she'll think I'm being dramatic or that I haven't moved on enough, which is kind of the same judgment I put on myself. I guess I don't fully trust that even the people who care about me can just sit with it the way you're describing, without turning it into advice or a pep talk.
therapist: It's really telling that the fear you have about Dara's reaction sounds almost identical to the voice you use on yourself — which suggests that inner critic may have actually been shaped by experiences of feeling like your feelings were too much for others to simply hold. Dara might surprise you, and she might not, but what strikes me is that you've never actually given her the chance to show up in this specific way. I'm wondering — what would it look like to share just a small, honest piece of this with her, not the whole weight of it at once, but enough to test whether that fear is based on evidence or expectation?

client: I think I could maybe tell her something small, like just that I've been having a harder time with the breakup than I've been letting on — but even imagining saying that out loud to her makes me feel kind of nauseous. It's like there's this fear that once I open that door even a little, I won't be able to control how much comes out, and then I'll feel exposed in a way I can't take back. I want to try it but I also really don't, if that makes sense.
therapist: That ambivalence — wanting something and dreading it at the same time — is actually a really healthy sign that you're considering something that genuinely matters to you, because we only feel that kind of pull around things that are real and important. The fear of losing control once the door opens makes complete sense, but I'd gently offer that you've been opening a door here today, little by little, and you've actually managed it really well without falling apart. What if the goal with Dara wasn't to open the door fully, but just to knock on it — one honest sentence, and then you get to decide what happens next?

client: That reframe actually helps a little — "knocking" feels less terrifying than opening, and I like that I'd still have some control over what happens next. But I'm already trying to figure out when I'd even do it, and I keep coming up with reasons why the timing is never quite right, which I'm aware is probably just avoidance. I think part of me is hoping that if I sit with the idea long enough, the courage will just show up on its own without me having to actually do anything.
therapist: You've just caught yourself in the avoidance pattern in real time, which is actually a really important skill — and you're right that courage rarely arrives on its own, it usually shows up *during* the scary thing rather than before it. The "waiting for the right moment" feeling is very similar to what keeps you out of that café, and it's worth noticing that the same protective mechanism is running in both places. I'm wondering — not when the perfect moment would be, but what the *smallest possible* version of that knock could look like, and whether there's one moment in the next few days where "imperfect timing" might actually be good enough?

client: Dara and I are getting coffee on Thursday, which is almost funny given everything, and I think that could be the moment even though my instinct is to say the timing is off because we'll be in public and it might get emotional. The smallest version I can imagine is just saying "I've been struggling more than I've shown" and then stopping there, not explaining everything, just that one sentence. I'm going to try to hold onto the "knocking" idea because it makes it feel like I'm still in control of the door, but I honestly don't know if I'll actually go through with it when I'm sitting across from her.
therapist: Thursday with Dara feels like exactly the right moment, and I love that you've already identified the one sentence — that's not a small thing, that's actually the whole experiment, and you've designed it really well. The uncertainty about whether you'll go through with it is completely normal, and I'd encourage you to hold that lightly rather than turning it into another thing to judge yourself for if it doesn't happen. Before Thursday, it might help to notice what comes up for you in the lead-up — not to force the courage, but just to get curious about what the resistance feels like when it arrives — and I'm wondering, what would you want to say to yourself in that moment right before you decide whether to knock or not?
